title: Song 5:1 — the Greek has a clause before “I am come into my garden” that the KJV and Hebrew lack
summary: The KJV verse begins “I am come into my garden”. Brenton’s Greek prints a sentence before it: let my kinsman come down into his garden and eat his fruit.
text: KJV Song of Solomon 5:1: “I am come into my garden, my sister, my spouse: I have gathered my myrrh with my spice; I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey; I have drunk my wine with my milk: eat, O friends; drink, yea, drink abundantly, O beloved.” Hebrew (WLC) 5:1: בָּ֣אתִי לְגַנִּי֮ אֲחֹתִ֣י כַלָּה֒ אָרִ֤יתִי מֹורִי֙ עִם־בְּשָׂמִ֔י אָכַ֤לְתִּי יַעְרִי֙ עִם־דִּבְשִׁ֔י שָׁתִ֥יתִי יֵינִ֖י עִם־חֲלָבִ֑י אִכְל֣וּ רֵעִ֔ים שְׁת֥וּ וְשִׁכְר֖וּ דֹּודִֽים׃ Brenton’s Greek 5:1: Καταβήτω ἀδελφιδός μου εἰς κῆπον αὐτοῦ, καὶ φαγέτω καρπὸν ἀκροδρύων αὐτοῦ· εἰσῆλθον εἰς κῆπόν μου ἀδελφή μου νύμφη· ἐτρύγησα σμύρναν μου μετὰ ἀρωμάτων μου, ἔφαγον ἄρτον μου μετὰ μέλιτός μου, ἔπιον οἶνόν μου μετὰ γάλακτός μου· φάγετε πλήσιοι καὶ πίετε, καὶ μεθύσθητε ἀδελφοί. Brenton’s own English (https://ebible.org/eng-Brenton/SNG05.htm) prints: “Let my kinsman come down into his garden, and eat the fruit of his choice berries. I am come into my garden, my sister, my spouse: I have gathered my myrrh with my spices; I have eaten my bread with my honey; I have drunk my wine with my milk. Eat, O friends, and drink; yea, brethren, drink abundantly.”. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/22/5/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/SNG05.htm.
reasoning: The Hebrew verse opens with בָּאתִי לְגַנִּי (“I have come to my garden”). The Greek verse has two sentences before that point is reached: Καταβήτω ἀδελφιδός μου εἰς κῆπον αὐτοῦ, καὶ φαγέτω καρπὸν ἀκροδρύων αὐτοῦ. The KJV therefore has one speaker arriving in the garden; the Greek page first prints an invitation, in the third person, for the beloved to come down to ‘his’ garden and eat its fruit, then the arrival. The KJV and Hebrew have no such opening clause.
scope: T applies to the clause quoted only. The verse is also not word for word the same at the end (the KJV has “honeycomb”, the Greek ἄρτον, ‘bread’); only the added opening clause is compared here. This compares the wording of three texts. It does not show which wording is original, and it does not say what the Hebrew word means beyond the words quoted. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. The Greek quoted is Brenton's printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original. Different English synonyms alone are not a difference in meaning, and a shared root does not settle context.

title: The Greek adds oath phrases at Song of Solomon 5:8 and 8:4
summary: Song of Solomon 5:8 and 8:4 appeal to Jerusalem's daughters. The KJV gives no basis for these oaths. The old Greek translation adds powers and forces of the field at 5:8. It adds forces of the field at 8:4.
text: KJV Song of Solomon 5:8: “I charge you, O daughters of Jerusalem, if ye find my beloved, that ye tell him, that I am sick of love.” Hebrew text 5:8: הִשְׁבַּ֥עְתִּי אֶתְכֶ֖ם בְּנֹ֣ות יְרוּשָׁלִָ֑ם אִֽם־תִּמְצְאוּ֙ אֶת־דֹּודִ֔י מַה־תַּגִּ֣ידוּ לֹ֔ו שֶׁחֹולַ֥ת אַהֲבָ֖ה אָֽנִי׃ Old Greek translation 5:8: Ὥρκισα ὑμᾶς θυγατέρες Ἱερουσαλὴμ ἐν ταῖς δυνάμεσι καὶ ἐν ταῖς ἰσχύσεσι τοῦ ἀγροῦ· ἐὰν εὕρητε τὸν ἀδελφιδόν μου, τί ἀπαγγείλητε αὐτῷ; ὅτι τετρωμένη ἀγάπης ἐγώ εἰμι. The English version of the old Greek translation (https://ebible.org/eng-Brenton/SNG05.htm) prints: “I have charged you, O daughters of Jerusalem, by the powers and the virtues of the field: if ye should find my kinsman, what are ye to say to him? That I am wounded with love.”. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/22/5/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/SNG05.htm. KJV Song of Solomon 8:4: “I charge you, O daughters of Jerusalem, that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, until he please.” Hebrew text 8:4: הִשְׁבַּ֥עְתִּי אֶתְכֶ֖ם בְּנֹ֣ות יְרוּשָׁלִָ֑ם מַה־תָּעִ֧ירוּ ׀ וּֽמַה־תְּעֹֽרְר֛וּ אֶת־הָאַהֲבָ֖ה עַ֥ד שֶׁתֶּחְפָּֽץ׃ Old Greek translation 8:4: Ὥρκισα ὑμᾶς θυγατέρες Ἱερουσαλὴμ ἐν ταῖς ἰσχύσεσι τοῦ ἀγροῦ· ἐὰν ἐγείρητε καὶ ἐὰν ἐξεγείρητε τὴν ἀγάπην ἕως ἂν θελήσῃ. The English version of the old Greek translation (https://ebible.org/eng-Brenton/SNG08.htm) prints: “I have charged you, ye daughters of Jerusalem, by the virtues of the field, that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, until he please.”. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/22/8/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/SNG08.htm.
reasoning: The Greek oath phrases add wording absent from the KJV and Hebrew text at these verses. The phrases differ: 5:8 names both powers and forces, while 8:4 names forces only. The existing 2:7 and 3:5 finding instead contrasts animal names with powers; these verses add an oath basis.
scope: Only the added oath wording at Song of Solomon 5:8 and 8:4 is compared. The different message/question wording at 5:8 is outside the finding. Sick and wounded are not treated as a separate meaning difference, and the Hebrew word is not defined here. The earlier oath record remains separate; repeated explanation is not counted as another finding. These digital editions do not show what all ancient copies contain or which wording came first. Other Hebrew copies were not checked. Sources name the Hebrew text and the old Greek translation used here. English in square brackets is the researcher’s rendering, not KJV wording or a dictionary definition.

title: Song 8:2 — the KJV has “who would instruct me”; the Greek has “the chamber of her that conceived me”
summary: At Song of Solomon 8:2, the KJV names “my mother's house, who would instruct me”. The old Greek translation names the house and the chamber of the woman who conceived her, without instruct.
text: KJV Song of Solomon 8:2: “I would lead thee, and bring thee into my mother's house, who would instruct me: I would cause thee to drink of spiced wine of the juice of my pomegranate.” Hebrew text 8:2: אֶנְהָֽגֲךָ֗ אֲבִֽיאֲךָ֛ אֶל־בֵּ֥ית אִמִּ֖י תְּלַמְּדֵ֑נִי אַשְׁקְךָ֙ מִיַּ֣יִן הָרֶ֔קַח מֵעֲסִ֖יס רִמֹּנִֽי׃ Old Greek translation 8:2: Παραλήψομαί σε, εἰσάξω σε εἰς οἶκον μητρός μου καὶ εἰς ταμεῖον τῆς συλλαβούσης με· ποτιῶ σε ἀπὸ οἴνου τοῦ μυρεψικοῦ, ἀπὸ νάματος ῥοῶν μου. The English version of the old Greek translation (https://ebible.org/eng-Brenton/SNG08.htm) prints: “I would take thee, I would bring thee into my mother's house, and into the chamber of her that conceived me; I would make thee to drink of spiced wine, of the juice of my pomegranates.”. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/22/8/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/SNG08.htm.
reasoning: The compared clause has teaching in the KJV and an added room in this Greek edition. The exact language quotations remain in the text field.
scope: Only this clause at Song of Solomon 8:2 is compared. The KJV wording is one reading of the Hebrew clause. This record does not exclude other readings or define the verb. title: Song 8:5 — “from the wilderness” in the KJV; the Greek has her “all white”
summary: At Song of Solomon 8:5, the KJV asks who comes from the wilderness while leaning on her beloved. The old Greek translation in the cited edition has all white and does not print wilderness.
text: KJV Song of Solomon 8:5: “Who is this that cometh up from the wilderness, leaning upon her beloved? I raised thee up under the apple tree: there thy mother brought thee forth: there she brought thee forth that bare thee.” Hebrew text 8:5: מִ֣י זֹ֗את עֹלָה֙ מִן־הַמִּדְבָּ֔ר מִתְרַפֶּ֖קֶת עַל־דֹּודָ֑הּ תַּ֤חַת הַתַּפּ֙וּחַ֙ עֹֽורַרְתִּ֔יךָ מָּה חִבְּלַ֣תְךָ אִמֶּ֔ךָ שָׁ֖מָּה חִבְּלָ֥ה יְלָדַֽתְךָ׃ Old Greek translation 8:5: Τίς αὕτη ἡ ἀναβαίνουσα λελευκανθισμένη, ἐπιστηριζομένη ἐπὶ τὸν ἀδελφιδὸν αὐτῆς; Ὑπὸ μῆλον ἐξήγειρά σε· ἐκεῖ ὠδίνησέ σε ἡ μήτηρ σου, ἐκεῖ ὠδίνησέ σε ἡ τεκοῦσά σε. The English version of the old Greek translation (https://ebible.org/eng-Brenton/SNG08.htm) prints: “Who is this that comes up all white, leaning on her kinsman? I raised thee up under an apple-tree; there thy mother brought thee forth; there she that bore thee brought thee forth.”. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/22/8/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/SNG08.htm.
reasoning: The compared KJV wording describes where she comes from. This Greek wording describes her appearance, using the term rendered all white in the linked English version.
scope: Only the quoted clause at Song of Solomon 8:5 in this Greek edition is compared. Other Greek editions were not checked. No claim is made about wording in all ancient copies. These digital editions do not show what all ancient copies contain or which wording came first. Other Hebrew copies were not checked.
